questions.questionText:
A car of mass 1,200 kg accelerates uniformly from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 8.0 s along a level road.
(a) Calculate the acceleration of the car. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the resultant forward force acting on the car. [2 marks]
(c) Calculate the distance travelled during these 8.0 s. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Uniform Acceleration & (b) Resultant Forward Force [4 marks]:** Given initial velocity **u = 5 m/s**, final velocity **v = 25 m/s**, and time **t = 8.0 s**, apply the first equation of linear kinematics **a = (v - u) ÷ t**: **a = (25 - 5) ÷ 8.0 = 20 ÷ 8.0 = 2.5 m/s²** forward [2 marks]. Next apply **Newton’s Second Law (F = m × a)** using car mass **m = 1,200 kg**: **F = 1,200 kg × 2.5 m/s² = 3,000 N** (or **3.0 kN** resultant net accelerating force!) [2 marks].

**(c) Distance Travelled During Uniform Acceleration [2 marks]:** Under steady constant acceleration, apply the average-velocity distance equation **s = ½(u + v) × t** (equally cleanly verified via **s = ut + ½at²**!). Using average velocity gives **s = ½ × (5 + 25) × 8.0 = 15 m/s × 8.0 s = 120 m**. Cross-checking with **s = (5 × 8) + ½(2.5)(8²) = 40 + 80 = 120 m** confirms exact mathematical consistency!

**Resultant vs Engine Driving Force Distinction:** Notice carefully why Part (b) labels 3,000 N the **resultant** force—if air drag and tyre rolling friction push backward with 800 N total resistance, the car engine itself must actually push forward with **3,000 + 800 = 3,800 N** to keep **3,000 N** net acceleration!

questions.questionText:
An electric pump raises 400 kg of water from a borehole 30 m deep to a raised tank in 40 s (g = 10 N/kg).
(a) Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained by the water. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the useful power of the pump. [2 marks]
(c) If the electrical input power is 4.0 kW, calculate the percentage efficiency of the pump. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Gravitational Potential Energy (GPE) & (b) Useful Output Power [4 marks]:** Rising water of mass **m = 400 kg** through vertical height **h = 30 m** (under **g = 10 N/kg**) gains **GPE = m × g × h = 400 × 10 × 30 = 120,000 J (120 kJ)** [2 marks]. Power measures rate of useful work done per second (**P = Work / Energy ÷ Time**); dividing by **t = 40 s** yields **Useful Output Power = 120,000 J ÷ 40 s = 3,000 W (3.0 kW)** [2 marks].

**(c) Percentage Efficiency of the Borehole Pump [2 marks]:** Convert units cleanly so input and output match (**both in kW or both in W!**): given **Electrical Input Power = 4.0 kW (4,000 W)** and **Useful Output Power = 3.0 kW (3,000 W)**, compute **Efficiency = (Useful Power Output ÷ Total Power Input) × 100% = (3.0 kW ÷ 4.0 kW) × 100% = 75%** (leaving 25%, or 1.0 kW, dissipated usefully-nowhere as winding heat, bearing friction, and pipe turbulence!).

**Common Unit-Mismatch Trap in Efficiency Calculations:** Never divide **3,000 W ÷ 4.0 kW** straight away yielding a comical **75,000% efficiency**! By **Law of Conservation of Energy**, real machines NEVER exceed **100% efficiency**, so spotting >100% should immediately alert you to convert **kW ↔ W** cleanly first!

questions.questionText:
A block of metal of mass 2.0 kg and specific heat capacity 400 J/(kg°C) is heated from 20°C to 75°C by an electric immersion heater rated 500 W.
(a) Calculate the thermal energy absorbed by the metal block. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the minimum time needed to heat the block assuming no heat loss. [2 marks]
(c) State why the actual time taken in a laboratory is longer. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Thermal Energy Absorbed & (b) Minimum Ideal Heating Time [4 marks]:** Given mass **m = 2.0 kg**, specific heat capacity **c = 400 J/(kg°C)**, and temperature rise **Δθ = 75°C - 20°C = 55°C**, apply **Q = m × c × Δθ**: **Q = 2.0 × 400 × 55 = 44,000 J (44 kJ)** [2 marks]. Since electrical heater power **P = Q ÷ t = 500 W (500 J/s)**, rearranging for time gives **t = Q ÷ P = 44,000 J ÷ 500 W = 88 s** (1 minute 28 seconds assuming 100% insulation!) [2 marks].

**(c) Why Real Laboratory Heating Takes Longer Than 88 s [1 mark]:** In a real school lab setup, **substantial thermal energy escapes continuously to surrounding air, laboratory bench, heater casing, and thermometer** via conduction, convection, and radiation—meaning only part of the 500 J supplied every second actually warms the metal block itself, extending heating time visibly past 88 s!

**Practical Exam Follow-Up & Specific Heat Interpretation:** Notice how **400 J/(kg°C)** tells us every kilogram of this metal (notice ~brass/copper sits near 380–400!) needs 400 Joules just to rise 1°C—nearly **ten times less energy** than water (**4,200 J/kg°C**), explaining why empty dry metal saucepans sear scorching hot far faster than full kettles of water! Lagging the metal block inside thick **expanded polystyrene foam** slashes thermal escape closer to theoretical 88 s.

questions.questionText:
Two resistors of 4.0 Ω and 12.0 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V d.c. battery.
(a) Calculate the combined resistance of the two resistors. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the total current drawn from the battery. [2 marks]
(c) Calculate the current flowing through the 4.0 Ω resistor. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Combined Parallel Resistance [2 marks]:** When resistors **R₁ = 4.0 Ω** and **R₂ = 12.0 Ω** sit wired in **parallel**, current splits cleanly across two paths so **combined resistance MUST end up smaller than the smallest branch (< 4.0 Ω)!** Apply **1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ = 1/4 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12 = 1/3**—remember to **INVERT the final fraction cleanly!** Giving **R_total = 3.0 Ω** (equivalently verified by product-over-sum: **(4 × 12) ÷ (4 + 12) = 48 ÷ 16 = 3.0 Ω**).

**(b) Total Battery Current & (c) Branch Current Through 4.0 Ω Resistor [4 marks]:** Apply **Ohm’s Law (I = V ÷ R)** across the entire circuit driven by **12 V**: **Total Current I_total = 12 V ÷ 3.0 Ω = 4.0 A** [2 marks]. Because components wired directly in **parallel share the identical full 12 V potential difference**, find current inside the **4.0 Ω branch** straight from **I₄ = V ÷ R₁ = 12 V ÷ 4.0 Ω = 3.0 A** [2 marks].

**Kirchhoff Current Conservation Cross-Check:** Check the remaining **12.0 Ω branch** immediately to catch arithmetic mistakes: **I₁₂ = 12 V ÷ 12.0 Ω = 1.0 A**, and **3.0 A + 1.0 A = 4.0 A exact total battery current**! Notice also the inverse ratio rule: the **3× lower resistance path (4 Ω vs 12 Ω) carries 3× larger current (3 A vs 1 A)**!

questions.questionText:
(a) State the two conditions required for total internal reflection to occur. [2 marks]
(b) Glass has a refractive index n = 1.50. Calculate its critical angle c. [2 marks]
(c) Give one practical application of total internal reflection. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Two Mandatory Conditions for Total Internal Reflection (TIR) [2 marks]:** Total internal reflection can NEVER occur unless **BOTH** conditions apply strictly simultaneously: **(1) Direction Condition:** the incident light ray must travel inside an **optically denser slow medium approaching a boundary with a less dense faster medium** (*e.g. glass → air or water → air, NEVER air → glass!*); and **(2) Angle Condition:** the **angle of incidence inside the denser medium must strictly exceed the critical angle (i > c)** so zero light escapes refracted out—100% bounces neatly back inside!

**(b) Calculating Glass Critical Angle c & (c) Practical Application [3 marks]:** At the critical angle **c**, the refracted ray skims right along the glass–air boundary at **r = 90°**, simplifying Snell’s Law cleanly to **sin(c) = 1 ÷ n**. Given refractive index **n = 1.50**: **sin(c) = 1 ÷ 1.50 = 0.6667**, taking inverse sine gives **c = sin⁻¹(0.6667) = 41.8°** (typically ~42° for standard crown glass!) [2 marks]. **Practical Applications:** High-speed **Optical Fibres** guiding internet laser pulses around bent underground cables, **45°–90° Periscope & Binocular Reflecting Prisms**, medical **endoscopes**, and sparkling faceted diamonds/roadside **cat’s-eye reflectors** [1 mark].

**Why 45° Glass Prisms Outshine Ordinary Silvered Mirrors in Periscopes:** Because light striking internal hypotenuse glass faces at **45° exceeds the 41.8° critical angle**, **100% of incident light reflects cleanly without ghostly double-glass reflections or dull tarnishing silver backing**, keeping sharp crisp images for cameras and binoculars indefinitely!

questions.questionText:
A uniform beam AB of length 4.0 m and weight 100 N is pivoted at its midpoint C (2.0 m). A boy weighing 400 N sits 1.5 m from C on the left side.
(a) Calculate the anticlockwise moment produced by the boy about C. [2 marks]
(b) How far to the right of C must a girl weighing 300 N sit to balance the beam horizontally? [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Boy’s Anticlockwise Turning Moment About Midpoint Pivot C [2 marks]:** Check first whether the uniform beam’s own **100 N weight** creates any turning moment: because the uniform 4.0 m beam’s **centre of gravity sits precisely at midpoint pivot C (0 m perpendicular lever distance!)**, the beam’s weight produces **zero turning moment** (*though pivot C pushes upward supporting beam + children!*). Calculating the boy’s anticlockwise moment on the left: **Moment = Force × Perpendicular Distance from Pivot = 400 N × 1.5 m = 600 N·m** anticlockwise.

**(b) Balancing Position for Girl Using Principle of Moments [3 marks]:** For the beam to rest balanced in **rotational equilibrium**, the **Principle of Moments** states **Total Clockwise Moments = Total Anticlockwise Moments** about pivot C: **300 N × d₂ = 600 N·m**. Dividing cleanly yields **d₂ = 600 ÷ 300 = 2.0 m to the right of pivot C**—placing the lighter girl right on the **extreme right end B** of the 4.0 m seesaw!

**Translational Equilibrium Check (Pivot Reaction Force):** Notice that complete mechanical equilibrium satisfies TWO rules simultaneously: **Sum of Clockwise = Sum of Anticlockwise Moments (600 = 600 N·m)** AND **Upward Pivot Reaction = Total Downward Weights = 400 N (boy) + 300 N (girl) + 100 N (beam weight) = 800 N upward**! Always verify units stay strictly **N·m** (force × metres, never cm without converting!).

questions.questionText: Describe a simple laboratory experiment to determine the density of a small irregularly shaped stone using a balance and a measuring cylinder. [5 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Step 1 & 2 — Measuring Mass and Initial Water Reading [2 marks]:** First ensure the irregular stone is **clean and completely dry**, then measure its accurate **mass m (in grams)** using a calibrated **electronic top-pan balance or beam balance** (zeroed cleanly first!) [1 mark]. Next pour enough clear water into a tall **graduated measuring cylinder** to cover the stone completely without splashing over the rim, place the cylinder flat on a level bench, and record initial **volume V₁ (in cm³)** reading strictly **at eye level to the bottom of the curved water meniscus** avoiding parallax error [1 mark].

**Step 3 to 5 — Submerged Volume Displacement & Density Calculation [3 marks]:** Tie a **fine thin thread** neatly around the stone and lower it **slowly gently down into the measuring cylinder** without splashing droplets up the walls, tapping lightly if needed so **zero trapped air bubbles** cling onto rough stone pores, until fully submerged. Record the new higher water volume **V₂ (cm³)** at eye level [1 mark]. Subtract cleanly to find true **stone volume V = V₂ - V₁**, then calculate **Density ρ = Mass ÷ Volume = m ÷ (V₂ - V₁)** in **g/cm³** (multiplying by 1,000 gives SI **kg/m³**!) [2 marks].

**Precautions & Floating-Object Adaptation (Cork Sinkers):** Notice why dipping dry before wetting matters—wet water weight falsely inflates mass! And if asked about a less-dense **floating cork**, attach a known-volume lead **sinker** first (*V_cork = V_both - V_water+sinker*) to drag it cleanly underwater, or use a brim-full **Eureka displacement can** cleanly for large stones too fat for narrow measuring cylinders.

questions.questionText:
A transformer connected to 230 V mains supplies 11.5 V to a school bell.
(a) Explain why the transformer core is made of laminated soft iron. [2 marks]
(b) If the primary coil has 2,400 turns, calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil. [2 marks]
(c) If the secondary current is 2.0 A and the transformer is 100% efficient, find the primary current. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Why Transformer Cores Use Laminated Soft Iron [2 marks]:** **Soft Iron** is chosen because it **magnetises and demagnetises effortlessly 50 times every second** with minimal **hysteresis energy loss**, channeling intense alternating magnetic flux cleanly from primary to secondary coils [1 mark]. Building that core from **thin insulated sheets ("laminations") glued side-by-side** rather than one solid iron block dramatically raises electrical resistance across the core, **slashing wasteful induced swirling eddy currents** that would otherwise overheat the core [1 mark].

**(b) Secondary Coil Turns & (c) Primary Input Current [4 marks]:** Apply the ideal **Transformer Voltage–Turns Equation (Vs / Vp = Ns / Np)**: given **Vp = 230 V**, **Vs = 11.5 V** (notice **step-down ratio 20 : 1**!), and **Np = 2,400 turns**, solve **Ns = Np × (Vs ÷ Vp) = 2,400 × (11.5 ÷ 230) = 2,400 × (1 ÷ 20) = 120 turns** [2 marks]. Next, assuming **100% efficiency (Power Input = Power Output → Vp × Ip = Vs × Is)** with **Is = 2.0 A**: **230 × Ip = 11.5 × 2.0 = 23.0 W**, giving **Ip = 23.0 ÷ 230 = 0.10 A** [2 marks].

**Physics Sanity Check — Why Transformers Never Work on Steady d.c. Batteries:** Notice cleanly why stepping **voltage DOWN 20×** simultaneously steps **current UP 20×** (*0.10 A → 2.0 A*), conserving total 23 W electrical power! Always remember transformers rely strictly on **continuously changing alternating magnetic flux (Faraday’s Law)**—wiring 230 V d.c. into the primary blows zero induced secondary voltage after switch-on and risks overheating primary copper windings.

questions.questionText:
A student fires a starting pistol 510 m from a cliff and hears the echo 3.0 s later.
(a) Calculate the speed of sound in air from these measurements. [3 marks]
(b) State two uses of ultrasound waves. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Speed of Sound Calculation Using Double Echo Path [3 marks]:** Remember carefully how sound echoes work: when the starting pistol cracks **510 m** from the vertical cliff, the sound wave travels **510 m outward TO the cliff AND 510 m back TO the student’s ears**, covering **Total Distance = 2 × 510 m = 1,020 m** before the echo returns at **t = 3.0 s** [1 mark]! Substituting cleanly into **Speed = Total Distance ÷ Total Time** gives **v = 1,020 m ÷ 3.0 s = 340 m/s** [2 marks]—matching standard warm-air speed cleanly!

**(b) Two Important Practical Uses of Ultrasound Waves (> 20,000 Hz) [2 marks]:** **(1) Medical Prenatal Foetal Scanning & Organ Diagnostics:** pulses of harmless high-frequency ultrasound bounce off boundaries between soft tissues, amniotic fluid, and bone inside a mother’s womb to construct safe live images **without dangerous ionising X-ray radiation** [1 mark]. **(2) SONAR Marine Depth Sounding & Industrial Flaw Detection / Ultrasonic Jewellery Cleaning:** ships bounce ultrasound echoes off seabeds/shoals (**d = ½vt**) to map ocean depths safely, engineers inspect steel railway axles for hidden hairline cracks, and gentle ultrasonic baths shake dirt safely off delicate watches and surgical instruments [1 mark].

**Avoiding the Half-Distance Exam Blunder:** The single most frequent error in Paper 2 echo problems is dividing **510 ÷ 3.0 = 170 m/s**—always sketch a quick arrow **Student → Cliff → Student** so you automatically double one-way distance (**2 × d = v × t**) before dividing by echo delay time!

questions.questionText:
Compare alpha (α), beta (β), and gamma (γ) radiations in terms of:
(a) nature/identity [3 marks],
(b) ionising power and penetrating ability [3 marks],
(c) one safety precaution when handling radioactive sources in a school laboratory [1 mark].
questions.explanation:
**(a) Physical Identity & Charge of Alpha, Beta, and Gamma Emissions [3 marks]:** **(1) Alpha (α) particle:** an identical fast-moving **Helium-4 nucleus (⁴_2 He)** packed tightly from **2 protons + 2 neutrons** carrying a hefty **+2 relative positive charge** and mass ~4 u [1 mark]. **(2) Beta (β⁻) particle:** a high-speed energetic **electron (⁰_-1 e)** ejected directly from the atomic nucleus when a neutron transforms cleanly into a proton + electron, carrying **-1 charge** and tiny negligible mass (~1/1840 u) [1 mark]. **(3) Gamma (γ) ray:** ultra-short-wavelength, high-frequency **electromagnetic wave/photon** carrying **zero mass and zero electric charge**, emitted when an excited daughter nucleus settles cleanly to lower energy [1 mark].

**(b) Ionising Power vs Penetrating Ability Trade-Off [3 marks]:** Notice the crisp inverse pattern: heavy, slow, doubly charged **Alpha (α)** smashes violently through air molecules producing **intense strong ionisation** right within ~3–5 cm, so it holds **very weak penetration**—stopped cleanly by a thin sheet of **paper or human outer dead skin**! Light fast **Beta (β)** causes **moderate ionisation** and penetrates **moderately** up to a few millimetres of **aluminium sheet**. Uncharged weightless **Gamma (γ)** barely interacts per centimetre (**very weak ionising power**) yet holds **extreme penetrating power**—needing several centimetres of **dense lead shielding or thick concrete walls** to attenuate strongly [3 marks].

**(c) School Laboratory Safety Handling Precaution [1 mark]:** Always lift radioactive sources strictly with **long-handled forceps/tongs** (never bare fingers—keeping inverse-square distance!), **never point sources toward eyes or classmates**, minimise exposure duration, and lock vials immediately inside **lead-lined storage safes** displaying standard radiation hazard trefoils—washing hands thoroughly afterward before eating.

questions.questionText:
(a) Distinguish between evaporation and boiling of a liquid. Give two differences. [4 marks]
(b) Explain why a swimmer feels cold when stepping out of water into a breeze. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Distinguishing Evaporation vs Boiling Across Key Characteristics [4 marks]:** First, **Temperature Range:** **Evaporation** occurs smoothly at **ANY temperature below boiling point** (wet laundry dries happily at 22°C!), whereas **Boiling** occurs strictly at **one exact fixed temperature (Boiling Point, 100°C for pure water at 1 atm)** [2 marks]. Second, **Location & Bubble Formation:** **Evaporation** takes place silently **strictly at the top liquid surface** with **zero bubbles**, whereas **Boiling** occurs violently **throughout the entire depth of liquid** forming vigorous rising vapour bubbles breaking upward [2 marks] (furthermore, boiling needs continuous heat input while evaporation cools the leftover liquid quietly!).

**(b) Why a Wet Swimmer Shivers Cold in a Breeze [2 marks]:** Stepping out onto poolside air, droplets clinging over warm skin **evaporate** rapidly because the **breeze sweeps humid saturated vapour continuously away**, accelerating evaporation rate sharply! During evaporation, **only the fastest, highest-kinetic-energy water molecules break free from surface attractions**, lowering the average kinetic energy of water film remaining behind and drawing substantial **Latent Heat of Vaporisation directly from the swimmer’s warm skin**—causing an immediate chilly cooling drop!

**Everyday Applications of Cooling by Evaporation:** Exactly this same kinetic cooling principle explains why traditional porous **clay water pots (*hari/zvirongo*)** keep drinking water delightfully chilled under hot shade, why sweating cools athletes safely during marathon runs, and why volatile medical spirit swabs feel icy on skin before injections.

questions.questionText:
A car battery has an EMF of 12 V and delivers a current of 3.0 A to two identical headlamps connected in parallel.
(a) Explain what is meant by "EMF of 12 V". [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the total resistance of the two lamps combined and the resistance of a single lamp. [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Meaning of "EMF = 12 V" [2 marks]:** Electromotive Force (EMF) measures total energy converted by a source per unit electric charge: an **EMF of 12 V** means the car battery converts **12 Joules of chemical energy into electrical energy for every 1 Coulomb of charge** pushed completely around the entire closed circuit (including any energy spent pushing across internal battery resistance!). Remember **1 Volt ≡ 1 Joule per Coulomb (1 V = 1 J/C)**.

**(b) Combined Resistance & Individual Parallel Headlamp Resistance [3 marks]:** Applying **Ohm’s Law** across the complete circuit carrying **I_total = 3.0 A** from **12 V**: **Total Combined Resistance R_total = V ÷ I_total = 12 V ÷ 3.0 A = 4.0 Ω** [1 mark]. Because **two identical headlamps (each resistance R)** sit wired in **parallel**, equal total current splits evenly (**1.5 A flowing through each lamp!**): directly from **R = V ÷ I_lamp = 12 V ÷ 1.5 A = 8.0 Ω**, OR via identical-resistors parallel rule **1/4.0 = 1/R + 1/R = 2/R → R = 8.0 Ω** [2 marks].

**Why Parallel Car Headlamps Beat Series Wiring:** Parallel wiring ensures BOTH headlamps shine cleanly at full bright **12 V rating** independently—crucially, if one front headlamp filament snaps open on a dark highway, the **second headlamp keeps blazing normally at 12 V** rather than plunging the entire vehicle into pitch darkness instantly as a broken series loop would!

questions.questionText: State Newton's three laws of motion and give one everyday example of Newton's First Law (inertia) in vehicle safety. [5 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Newton’s Three Laws of Motion Clearly Stated [3 marks]:** **Newton’s First Law (Law of Inertia):** Every object remains stationary or continues moving steadily in a **straight line at constant speed** unless compelled to change that state by an unbalanced **external resultant force** [1 mark]. **Newton’s Second Law (F = ma):** The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the **net resultant force** acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass (or strictly: resultant force equals **rate of change of linear momentum**) [1 mark]. **Newton’s Third Law (Action–Reaction Pairs):** Whenever Body A exerts a force upon Body B, Body B simultaneously exerts an **equal and strictly opposite force back upon Body A** (acting on *two different bodies*!) [1 mark].

**Vehicle Safety Application of Newton’s First Law (Inertia & Seatbelts) [2 marks]:** Imagine a minibus cruising briskly at **80 km/h** along the Harare–Bulawayo highway when the driver slams emergency brakes or hits an obstacle, halting the metal chassis abruptly within fractions of a second! By **Newton’s First Law**, belted-less passengers carry **forward inertia**—no direct braking force touches their bodies immediately, so passengers keep hurtling forward at **80 km/h** straight toward the windscreen and dashboard! Wearing **locked inertia-reel seatbelts** (alongside crumple zones and airbags) applies a gradual controlled backward **resultant stopping force** safely across strong shoulder/pelvis bones, extending impact duration to protect fragile skulls and spines cleanly!

**Clearing Up the Common Third-Law Action/Reaction Confusion:** Note sharply in Paper 2 that Earth pulling a book down (gravity) and a table pushing that same book up (normal reaction) are **NOT** a Newton III pair (*they act on the SAME book!*); true Newton III pairs ALWAYS act on **two separate interacting objects** (*Earth pulls Book down ↔ Book pulls Earth up*!).

questions.questionText:
A rectangular brick measures 20 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm and weighs 25 N.
(a) Calculate the maximum pressure it can exert on a table (in N/cm² and in Pa). [3 marks]
(b) Calculate the minimum pressure it can exert on the table (in N/cm²). [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Maximum Pressure in N/cm² and Pascals (Pa = N/m²) [3 marks]:** Pressure obeys **P = Force ÷ Contact Area (P = F / A)**, meaning a fixed weight (**25 N**) produces **MAXIMUM pressure when rested vertically upright onto its SMALLEST rectangular face**! Selecting the two smallest dimensions (**10 cm × 5 cm**) gives **Minimum Area A_min = 10 × 5 = 50 cm²**. Thus **P_max = 25 N ÷ 50 cm² = 0.50 N/cm²** [2 marks]. To convert into **SI Pascals (N/m²)** carefully, remember **1 m² = 100 cm × 100 cm = 10,000 cm²**: **A_min = 50 ÷ 10,000 = 0.0050 m²**, giving **P_max = 25 N ÷ 0.0050 m² = 5,000 Pa (5.0 kPa)** [1 mark] (quick check: multiply N/cm² cleanly by **10,000**!).

**(b) Minimum Pressure Exerted Lying Flat [2 marks]:** Conversely, **MINIMUM pressure occurs when lying flat upon its LARGEST face** spreading weight broadly (**20 cm × 10 cm**). Calculating **Maximum Area A_max = 20 × 10 = 200 cm²**, compute **P_min = 25 N ÷ 200 cm² = 0.125 N/cm²** [2 marks] (equivalently **1,250 Pa**—precisely one-quarter of maximum upright pressure!).

**Real-World Engineering Applications of Pressure Control:** Precisely this **P = F / A** principle explains why sharp knives concentrate modest arm force onto hair-thin blade edges slashing high cutting pressure easily, whereas wide heavy caterpillar tractor tracks and soft wide camel feet maximise ground contact area **A** so heavy machines glide cleanly over muddy fields and desert sand without sinking!

questions.questionText:
(a) Draw/describe the truth table of a 2-input NOR gate. [2 marks]
(b) Explain how a thermistor can be used in a potential-divider circuit as an automatic fire alarm trigger. [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Truth Table & Behaviour of a 2-Input NOR Gate [2 marks]:** A **NOR gate** operates as an **OR gate followed directly by a NOT inverter** (**Q = NOT(A OR B)**). Checking all four binary input combinations (**A, B → Output Q**): **(0, 0) → Output = 1 (HIGH)**; **(0, 1) → Output = 0 (LOW)**; **(1, 0) → Output = 0 (LOW)**; and **(1, 1) → Output = 0 (LOW)**. In words: a NOR gate outputs **HIGH (1) ONLY when BOTH inputs stay LOW (0)**—whenever *either* or *both* inputs go HIGH, the output drops immediately to **0**!

**(b) NTC Thermistor Potential Divider as an Automatic Fire Alarm Trigger [3 marks]:** Connect a **Negative Temperature Coefficient (NTC) thermistor** in series with a fixed protective **variable resistor** across a 6 V d.c. supply, taking output voltage across the fixed bottom resistor (or wiring the thermistor on the top half feeding an inverting/transistor relay buzzer!). Under cool normal room air, the **thermistor holds VERY HIGH resistance**, absorbing nearly all supply voltage so bottom output sits safely **LOW (< 0.7 V)** leaving the buzzer silent [1.5 marks]. As fire flames heat the room sharply, the **NTC thermistor’s resistance plunges dramatically**, letting far more current surge through so **potential difference rises steeply across the bottom resistor**—switching a transistor/relay ON cleanly to sound the loud **fire alarm siren** automatically! [1.5 marks].

**Alternative Wiring Awareness for Paper 2 Circuit Diagrams:** Remember carefully how **NTC thermistor resistance drops as temperature rises** (*opposite to glowing hot filament wires!*): if examiners draw the output voltmeter *across the thermistor itself*, rising temperature makes V_out **FALL** cleanly instead of rising—so read circuit component positions first before deciding whether voltage rises or falls!

questions.questionText: Describe an experiment to measure the specific heat capacity of water using an electrical immersion heater, thermometer, beaker, stopwatch, and joulemeter (or ammeter & voltmeter). [5 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Setup & Measured Physical Quantities [3 marks]:** Weigh a clean dry well-insulated copper or polystyrene **beaker/calorimeter empty** (**m₁**), pour in clean cold water, and reweigh to determine exact **water mass m = m₂ - m₁ (converted cleanly to kg)** [1 mark]. Wrap thick **lagging insulation** around sides and lid to cut heat escape, immerse an **electric immersion heater** plus stirred **thermometer** completely inside water, and read careful steady **initial water temperature θ₁ (°C)** [1 mark]. Wire heater through a calibrated **joulemeter** (or series **ammeter I**, parallel **voltmeter V**, and **stopwatch t**) [1 mark].

**Heating Procedure, Final Reading & Calculation Formula [2 marks]:** Switch ON the heater while stirring gently and uniformly for ~5–8 minutes; switch OFF, stir briefly so thermometer peaks steadily at highest **final temperature θ₂ (°C)**, and record total **electrical energy supplied E (from joulemeter in Joules, OR calculated via E = V × I × t)** [1 mark]. Assuming negligible calorimeter/heat loss (**Electrical Energy Supplied = Thermal Energy Gained by Water → E = m × c × (θ₂ - θ₁)**), solve directly for specific heat capacity: **c = E ÷ [m × (θ₂ - θ₁)]** (or **c = VIt ÷ [m(θ₂ - θ₁)]** in **J/(kg°C)**) [1 mark].

**Systematic Experimental Error Analysis:** Notice why experimental lab values for water often overshoot true **4,200 J/(kg°C)** slightly (e.g. measuring ~4,450 J/(kg°C)!): inevitably some **electrical energy E leaks out** warming the beaker, heater coil, and surrounding room air—increasing measured **E** needed for a given Δθ, inflating **c = E / (m Δθ)** upward unless lidded polystyrene insulation and small cooling corrections are applied.

questions.questionText:
An object 2.0 cm tall is placed 15 cm in front of a convex (converging) lens of focal length 10 cm.
(a) Use the lens formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v to find the image distance v. [3 marks]
(b) State three properties of the image formed (real/virtual, upright/inverted, size). [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Thin Lens Equation Step-by-Step Calculation for Image Distance v [3 marks]:** List known distances clearly using the real-is-positive sign convention: focal length of converging (convex) lens **f = +10 cm**, object distance **u = +15 cm**. Substitute into **1/f = 1/u + 1/v**: **1/10 = 1/15 + 1/v**. Rearrange carefully subtracting fractions using common denominator **30**: **1/v = 1/10 - 1/15 = 3/30 - 2/30 = 1/30**, inverting cleanly gives **Image Distance v = +30 cm** on the far side of the lens!

**(b) Three Complete Image Characteristics & Magnification Check [3 marks]:** Checking both sign and ratio **m = v ÷ u = 30 cm ÷ 15 cm = 2.0×**: **(1) Nature — REAL:** positive **v (+30 cm)** confirms refracted rays physically converge on the opposite side of the lens and can be focused sharply onto a white screen; **(2) Orientation — INVERTED:** all single-lens real images sit upside down; and **(3) Size — MAGNIFIED (ENLARGED 2×):** since **v > u**, an object **2.0 cm** tall projects as a crisp inverted image standing **2 × 2.0 cm = 4.0 cm tall**!

**Ray-Zone Cross-Check (10 cm < u = 15 cm < 20 cm):** Check immediately against the five classic Convex Lens object zones: because **15 cm sits strictly between f (10 cm) and 2f (20 cm)**, theory guarantees the image MUST sit **beyond 2f (> 20 cm — verified at 30 cm!)** and MUST be **Real, Inverted, and Magnified**—matching optical **slide and cinema projectors**!

questions.questionText:
A copper rod rests across two bare horizontal rails inside a strong magnetic field directed vertically downwards. When a battery is connected across the rails, the rod rolls sideways.
(a) Name the physical effect demonstrated. [1 mark]
(b) State two ways to increase the force pushing the rod. [2 marks]
(c) State one way to reverse the direction of motion. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Naming the Physical Phenomenon & Direction Rule [1 mark]:** Rolling sideways instantly when connected to the battery demonstrates the **Motor Effect (Catapult Effect)**—a current-carrying conductor placed perpendicular across an external magnetic field experiences a lateral mechanical **electromagnetic force** predicted accurately by **Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule** (*Thumb = Motion/Force, First finger = Magnetic Field N→S, Second finger = Conventional Current +→-*).

**(b) Two Ways to Strengthen Force & (c) Way to Reverse Roll Direction [3 marks]:** **(b) Increasing Force Magnitude (F = B × I × L):** **(1) Increase electric current I** flowing through the copper rod (*using higher-EMF battery cells or reducing circuit variable resistance*); and **(2) Increase magnetic field strength B** (*bringing stronger neodymium/horse-shoe magnet poles closer together around the copper rod*) [2 marks]. **(c) Reversing Direction of Motion:** either **reverse battery terminals (+ ↔ -)** to flip current direction OR **flip magnet poles (N ↔ S)** vertically upside down—NEVER flip *both* simultaneously because two reversals cancel out keeping motion unchanged! [1 mark].

**Industrial Motor Link & Why Only One Flip Reverses Spin:** Notice how d.c. electric motors harness that exact same lateral motor force spinning rectangular copper loops inside curved magnets—and require **split-ring commutators** specifically to flip coil current every half-turn so torque pushes steadily forward rather than rocking helplessly back and forth!

questions.questionText:
Explain why:
(a) small gaps are left between steel railway tracks, [2 marks]
(b) power lines hang loosely in summer, [2 marks]
(c) double-glazed windows keep rooms warmer in winter. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Expansion Gaps Left Between Steel Railway Tracks [2 marks]:** Metals expand measurably in length when absorbing midday solar heat (**thermal linear expansion** as atomic vibrations widen average spacing). Leaving calculated small **expansion gaps** (joined loosely with slotted fishplates) gives steel rails open room to **lengthen safely on scorching 40°C summer afternoons**—without those gaps, colossal internal compressive forces build up, **buckling heavy tracks sideways** and derailing passing trains!

**(b) Overhead Copper/Aluminium Power Lines Hung Loosely in Summer [2 marks]:** Technicians deliberately leave slack **droop/sag** when stringing overhead cables in warm weather because when **bitter cold winter nights (~0°C) hit, metal lines contract noticeably shorter**. Had engineers pulled cables drum-tight in blazing summer sun, winter thermal **contraction** would generate immense tensile snapping tension tearing cables clean off steel pylon insulators!

**(c) Double-Glazed Windows Conserving Room Warmth in Winter [2 marks]:** Double-glazed windows sandwich a thin sealed layer of **trapped dry air (or low-conductivity argon gas) between twin glass panes**. First, still **air is a terribly poor thermal conductor**, slashing conductive heat leakage outward dramatically compared to single glass; second, sealing that narrow ~1–2 cm pocket restricts swirling **convection currents** sharply, keeping costly indoor heater warmth trapped efficiently indoors!

questions.questionText:
A stone of mass 0.5 kg is thrown vertically upwards at 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). Neglecting air resistance:
(a) Calculate its initial kinetic energy. [2 marks]
(b) Use conservation of energy to calculate the maximum height reached. [3 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Initial Kinetic Energy (KE) at Launch [2 marks]:** Apply **Kinetic Energy KE = ½ × m × v²** cleanly using stone mass **m = 0.5 kg** and launch speed **v = 20 m/s** (remember to square velocity ONLY—never square mass!): **KE = ½ × 0.5 × (20)² = 0.25 × 400 = 100 J**.

**(b) Maximum Vertical Height via Conservation of Energy [3 marks]:** Neglecting air friction drag, the **Principle of Conservation of Mechanical Energy** dictates that as the stone rises slowing down to momentary zero speed (**v = 0 → KE = 0 J**) at its peak apex, **100% of initial 100 J Kinetic Energy transforms cleanly into Gravitational Potential Energy (GPE = m × g × h)**. Setting **0.5 × 10 × h = 100 J** simplifies to **5 × h = 100**, solving cleanly for **Maximum Height h = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 m**!

**Mass-Independence Check via Kinematics:** Cross-checking cleanly with kinematics equation **v² = u² + 2as** (**0 = 20² - 2×10×h → 20h = 400 → h = 20 m**) yields identical 20 m completely independent of stone mass! In real outdoor throws, air resistance drains slight mechanical energy into thermal air warming, capping true physical height modestly under 20 m.
